item.title: Pepsi's Ad Showed a Fighter Jet. He Sent $700,000.
item.description:
Pepsi's ad showed a fighter jet as a prize ✈️ so a student sent Pepsi a $700,000 check.
The 1996 ad said the Harrier jet cost 7,000,000 Pepsi Points. The rules let you buy points for 10 cents each.
He got investors, mailed 15 points and a check for the rest. Pepsi sent it back and said the jet was a joke, and a judge agreed in 1999.
Would you have tried it? 👇

item.title: Piggly Wiggly's Founder Tried to Beat Wall Street
item.description:
Piggly Wiggly's founder bet $10 million against Wall Street 📈 and invented the way you shop today.
In 1916 Clarence Saunders opened the first self-service grocery store in Memphis: turnstile, basket, pick your own food.
When traders bet his stock would fall, he borrowed about $10 million and bought most of the shares. The price shot from $75 to $124 by noon. Then the stock exchange stopped trading, and he went bankrupt.
Was he robbed, or did he push too far? 👇
⚠️ Dramatised illustration, real facts. Not investment advice. Follow @sneakydealstv for a new sneaky deal every day.
#pigglywiggly #shortsqueeze #businesshistory #wallstreet #sneakydeals

item.title: This Man Bought $3,000 of Pudding for Free Flights
item.description:
This man bought 12,150 pudding cups to earn free flights ✈️ The Pudding Guy's airline miles loophole is real.
In 1999 a Healthy Choice promo gave airline miles for barcodes. The cheapest item? Pudding, about 25 cents a cup.
He spent just over $3,000, had Salvation Army volunteers peel the labels in exchange for the pudding, and got more than 1.2 million miles.
Would you have spotted this loophole? 👇
⚠️ Dramatised illustration, real facts. Follow @sneakydealstv for a new sneaky deal every day.
#puddingguy #frequentflyer #businesshistory #loophole #sneakydeals

item.title: Disney Secretly Bought a Swamp Using Fake Names
item.description:
Disney secretly bought a swamp using fake names 🐊 One fake company was called "M.T. Lott"... say it fast.
Walt Disney wanted a huge park in Florida, but if sellers heard his name, prices would explode. So his team bought land through companies with harmless names, for under $200 an acre.
They gathered more than 27,000 acres, about twice the size of Manhattan, before a reporter cracked the secret in 1965.
Smart business or a dirty trick? 👇
